title: Contemplation is waking up
hookLine: for Merton, contemplation is being fully awake to the life you've been given
tomorrow: the false self and the true self

lines: HOME, AND YOU DON'T REMEMBER THE DRIVE.
cards: You've driven home and realized you don't remember a single turn. You've eaten a whole meal and couldn't say what it tasted like. You've sat with someone you love and been somewhere else entirely.
A lot of life runs on autopilot. It's easy to assume the spiritual life means adding something on top: more prayers, more feelings, more effort. Thomas Merton said something stranger.
The deepest prayer isn't adding anything. It's waking up to what's already here.

teach.b: First, Merton's definition. In New Seeds of Contemplation, from 1961, he calls contemplation the highest expression of our spiritual life, then says what it is: that same life, wide awake and aware that it's alive.
A kind of spiritual wonder, he says, a deep gratitude for being. Not a trance. Not a special feeling.
Not an escape from the world. Awake.
Second, you can't force a waking. Merton describes it as an awakening to the real in everything that is real, and no method switches it on. You can't wake yourself up by trying harder.
But you can open the curtains, put the phone in another room, stop hitting snooze. Silence, prayer and attention are the curtains. The waking comes when it comes.
Third, not only for monks. Merton's first version, Seeds of Contemplation, came out in 1949, written from inside the cloister. When he reworked it twelve years later, he widened the door.
A parent at the stove can be awake. So can a student on a bus. So could the old farmer at Ars you met a few weeks ago, looking and being looked at.
Saint Paul quotes what may be an early Christian hymn, in the Douay-Rheims: "Rise thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead: and Christ shall enlighten thee."
The Greek verb for rise there is the same one used for raising the dead. For Merton, the sleep isn't at night. It's the half-attention people live in all day.
Waking up is the prayer, and it can start with the next thing you do, done with your whole self.

how: Catholics practice contemplative prayer in many forms, from silent time before the Blessed Sacrament to centering prayer and lectio divina, and the Catechism describes contemplation as a gaze of faith fixed on Jesus.

s: for Merton, contemplation is a special trance
he says it's not a trance or an escape, but life itself, wide awake.
Merton says the right technique will switch contemplation on

games.q: you're Merton, twelve years after your first book on contemplation, written inside the cloister. reworking it, who do you say it's for?
o: anyone, inside the cloister or out
games.why: New Seeds widens the door: waking up to your own life isn't reserved for the monastery.

practice: Pick something right in front of you, your hands, a cup, the window, and look at it as if you'd never seen it: its color, its weight, the light on it, coming back whenever your mind drifts to plans.
Then feel your breathing and know: I'm alive, right now. If you pray, you can stay there, awake, in God's presence.

wordCard.voice: Egeire. The Greek word for 'rise' or 'wake up,' also used for raising the dead, and for Merton, the deepest prayer: being fully awake to the life you've been given. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: wake up, sleeper (Ephesians 5:14). egeire is also the verb for raising the dead.

carryVoice: Your line: wake up. A dish, a cup of coffee: anything can be done fully awake. Two hundred seventy-seven days in.
